steps.explanation:
A run differs from a walk in one way: there are moments when no foot touches the ground. This fox runs in 6 Frames, and its key poses are the two leaps, one for each foot.

In Frame 2 the fox is in the air, stretched out with its legs reaching forward and back. Its feet are a pixel off the bottom row.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png)

Frame 5 is the second leap, for the other foot. It is also in the air, but the body tips up instead of stretching out. Two leaps that differ a little keep the run from looking mechanical.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png)

Frame 1 comes just before the first stride. The fox is gathered up, body round and legs tucked under it, ready to push off.

Turn on **Onion skin** (O) to see the Frames on either side.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png)

Frame 3 lands the first leap: the feet are back on the bottom row and the legs pull in under the body.

![Frame 2](examples/frame-2.png) ![Frame 3](examples/frame-3.png) ![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png)

Frame 4 gathers the fox up for the second stride. Compare it with Frame 1: the same bunched pose, with the legs the other way round.

![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png) ![Frame 4](examples/frame-4.png)

Frame 6 brings the fox back from the second stride to Frame 1, closing the loop. Press **Play preview** (P) to watch it run. At 10 Frames a second, 6 Frames make a quick, light stride.

![Frame 5](examples/frame-5.png) ![Frame 6](examples/frame-6.png) ![Frame 1](examples/frame-1.png)
